text: Ettore Bugatti, an Italian-born industrial designer, founded the French automobile manufacturer Bugatti in 1909 in Molsheim, Alsace, which was part of the German Empire from 1871 to 1919. The company was renowned for its exceptional design beauty and engineering precision, reflecting the artistic legacy of Ettore’s family, particularly his father Carlo Bugatti, a prominent Art Nouveau designer. Bugatti cars, such as the Type 35 Grand Prix cars, the Type 41 "Royale," the Type 57 "Atlantic," and the Type 55 sports car, achieved significant success in racing, including winning the first Monaco Grand Prix in 1929 and securing victories in the Targa Florio from 1925 to 1929. Jean-Pierre Wimille won the 24 Hours of Le Mans twice—once in 1937 with Robert Benoist and again in 1939 with Pierre Veyron—marking the final major racing triumph, achieved with minimal resources. The company also developed the Bugatti 100P airplane, designed by Louis de Monge, which never flew. Ettore Bugatti designed the Autorail Bugatti, a motorised railcar, and emphasized elegant engineering, such as hand-scraped engine blocks, guilloché finishes, and axles with spring passages, while famously stating that "weight was the enemy" and criticizing competitors like Bentley for focusing on durability. The death of Ettore Bugatti in 1947 and his son Jean in 1939, who died while testing a Type 57 tank-bodied race car, severely impacted the company. World War II destroyed the Molsheim factory, and despite plans for a new factory in Levallois and development of the Type 73 road and racing cars—only five of which were built—the company ceased operations in 1952 after producing fewer than 8,000 vehicles. In 1963, Bugatti’s airplane parts business was sold to Hispano-Suiza, which was later acquired by Snecma, and in 1977, Snecma merged with Messier to form Messier-Bugatti. In 1987, Italian entrepreneur Romano Artioli acquired the Bugatti brand and established Bugatti Automobili S.p.A., commissioning Giampaolo Benedini to design a factory in Campogalliano, Italy, which opened in 1990. The first production model, the EB110 GT, featured a 3.5-litre quad-turbocharged 60° V12 engine, a six-speed gearbox, and four-wheel drive, with an initial aluminium honeycomb chassis later replaced by a carbon fibre one under Nicola Materazzi. Mauro Forghieri served as technical director from 1993 to 1994. The EB112 prototype was unveiled in 1993. Michael Schumacher, a seven-time Formula One World Champion, owned an EB110, which he sold after a 1994 crash. Poor economic conditions led to the company’s closure in September 1995, with a US-specific "Bugatti America" model in development. Dauer Racing acquired the EB110 license in 1997 to produce five refined EB110 SS models. The Campogalliano factory was later sold to a furniture company that became defunct. B Engineering, founded by former employees, built the Edonis using EB110 SS components. Volkswagen Group acquired the Bugatti brand in 1998. Giorgetto Giugiaro designed the EB118 concept, a coupé with a 408-kilowatt W-18 engine, debuted at the 1998 Paris Auto Show and shown in Geneva and Tokyo. The EB 218 and 18/3 Chiron concepts followed in 1999. Bugatti began regular production with the Veyron 16.4 in September 2005 at the Molsheim assembly studio, and sold its last Veyron Grand Sport Vitesse, named La Finale, on 23 February 2015. The Chiron, a mid-engined, two-seated sports car designed by Achim Anscheidt, succeeded the Veyron and was first revealed at the Geneva Motor Show on 1 March 2016. In February 2024, Bugatti announced a successor to the Chiron using a V16 hybrid-electric powertrain, confirmed as the Tourbillon in June 2024. The company's headquarters are located at 48°31′32″N 07°30′01″E. The name is currently owned by Bugatti Rimac since 2021. A film about the founding of Bugatti is being produced by Andrea Iervolino. A rare 1937 Type 57S Atalante, originally owned by Earl Howe, was found in 2009 and is notable for its intact original equipment. A 1925 Bugatti Brescia Type 22, recovered from Lake Maggiore in 2009 after 75 years underwater, was purchased by the Mullin Museum in 2010 for $351,343.
